clinicalPearls: A persistent or intermittent painless sensation of a lump or tightness in the throat without a true swallowing difficulty
The sensation is typically relieved rather than worsened by swallowing food, and there is no dysphagia to solids or liquids
It is a common and usually benign complaint, but true dysphagia, pain or weight loss should prompt urgent evaluation
Associations include laryngopharyngeal reflux, postnasal drip, anxiety and cricopharyngeal muscle dysfunction
Examination of the throat and neck, including laryngoscopy, is used to exclude structural or mucosal disease
Reassurance, treatment of reflux and speech and language therapy help many patients
reference.pathophysiology: Globus pharyngeus is a sensory symptom whose mechanism is incompletely understood and probably multifactorial. Proposed contributors include heightened pharyngeal sensitivity, laryngopharyngeal reflux causing mucosal irritation, increased upper oesophageal sphincter tone or cricopharyngeal dysfunction, and psychological factors such as anxiety that amplify throat awareness. It is a functional sensation in most cases, but the same complaint can occasionally herald structural pathology, which is why alarm features must be excluded.
additionalInvestigations: History focused on distinguishing globus from true dysphagia
Head and neck examination including flexible laryngoscopy
Assessment for reflux and postnasal drip
Endoscopy or contrast swallow if alarm features are present
Thyroid assessment where a neck swelling is suspected
redFlags: True dysphagia, odynophagia or food sticking
Weight loss, neck mass or persistent hoarseness
Referred otalgia with a smoking or alcohol history
reference.prognosis: The benign functional form is not dangerous and often improves with reassurance and treatment of contributing factors, though symptoms can be persistent or recurrent.
pitfalls: Attributing symptoms to globus when true dysphagia or alarm features are present
Missing an upper aerodigestive tract malignancy in a smoker
Failing to address reflux or anxiety that perpetuate the sensation
management: Firm reassurance once laryngoscopy and examination have excluded structural or mucosal disease, as the functional form is benign
Treat contributing laryngopharyngeal reflux with lifestyle modification, alginates and a trial of a proton pump inhibitor
Manage postnasal drip and any contributing rhinosinusitis
Refer for speech and language therapy addressing laryngeal muscle tension and vocal habits
Address associated anxiety with explanation and psychological approaches such as cognitive behavioural therapy where relevant
Escalate to urgent endoscopy or contrast swallow if alarm features develop, namely true dysphagia, throat pain or weight loss
